s.line: You will remember there was no road—not even a pathway—between the castle of the Wicked Witch and the Emerald City.
s.note: בֵּין … לְבֵין = "between … and". In careful writing the second item gets לְבֵין; in speech you also hear בֵּין … וּבֵין or simply בֵּין … וְ…. דֶּרֶךְ is usually feminine (דֶּרֶךְ אֲרֻכָּה), which is why הָיְתָה is feminine here.

s.line: When the four travelers went in search of the Witch she had seen them coming, and so sent the Winged Monkeys to bring them to her.
s.note: אַרְבַּעַת הַמְּטַיְּלִים = "the four travelers": with a definite noun, the number goes into construct form (אַרְבָּעָה → אַרְבַּעַת), as in שְׁלֹשֶׁת הַיְּלָדִים. רָאֲתָה אוֹתָם מִתְקָרְבִים: after "see", Hebrew uses a present participle the way English uses "-ing": "saw them approaching".

s.line: It was much harder to find their way back through the big fields of buttercups and yellow daisies than it was being carried.
s.note: לְהִנָּשֵׂא is the nif'al infinitive of נָשָׂא (carry): "to be carried". The same nif'al also means "to get married" (נִשְּׂאָה לְ…), a formal word you see in the news. מֵאֲשֶׁר = "than" before a verb or clause; before a noun you just use מִ: קָשֶׁה מִזֶּה.

w: שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם|that they must|~lit. that on them (it is)
s.line: They knew, of course, they must go straight east, toward the rising sun;
s.note: עֲלֵיהֶם לָלֶכֶת = "they must go", literally "it is on them to go". עָלַי, עָלֶיךָ, עָלֵינוּ + infinitive is a common way to express duty: עָלֶיךָ לְהַחְלִיט (you have to decide). מִזְרָחָה: the ending ָה means "toward": צָפוֹנָה, הַבַּיְתָה (homeward).

w: יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out|~lit. went out to the road
s.line: and they started off in the right way.
But at noon, when the sun was over their heads, they did not know which was east and which was west,
s.note: שֶׁמֶשׁ is feminine in modern Hebrew (הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ הָיְתָה, הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ הָעוֹלָה above). צָהֳרַיִם has the "dual" ending ַיִם, like עַרְבַּיִם (dusk); אַחֲרֵי הַצָּהֳרַיִם = afternoon, and Israelis say צָהֳרַיִם טוֹבִים as a greeting.

w: הָלְכוּ לְאִבּוּד|got lost|~idiom: lit. went to loss
s.line: and that was the reason they were lost in the great fields.
s.note: הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = got lost, the everyday expression for people and for things: הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת הָלְכוּ לְאִבּוּד (the keys got lost). Compare אִבֵּד אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ (lost the way), which you will meet in a moment.

w: בְּכָל זֹאת|nevertheless|~idiom: lit. in all this
s.line: They kept on walking, however, and at night the moon came out and shone brightly.
So they lay down among the sweet smelling yellow flowers and slept soundly until morning—all but the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.
s.note: יָשְׁנוּ שֵׁנָה עֲמֻקָּה: verb + noun from the same root, as in קָד קִידָה; the adjective carries the meaning ("slept soundly"). רֵיחָנִי = fragrant, from רֵיחַ (smell). חוּץ מִ… = except; note that the מִ is repeated before each item.

s.line: The next morning the sun was behind a cloud,
s.note: שֶׁלְּמָחֳרָת = "of the next day" (looking back on the past), while מָחָר is "tomorrow" from today: בַּיּוֹם שֶׁלְּמָחֳרָת = the following day. לְמָחֳרָת on its own also works: לְמָחֳרָת הֵם יָצְאוּ = the next day they set out.

s.line: but they started on, as if they were quite sure which way they were going.
“If we walk far enough,” said Dorothy, “I am sure we shall sometime come to some place.”
s.note: אִם נֵלֵךְ: after אִם about the future, Hebrew uses the future tense ("if we will walk"), not the present as in English. אֵיזֶשֶׁהוּ = "some (or other)", feminine אֵיזוֹשֶׁהִי: אֵיזֶשֶׁהוּ מָקוֹם, אֵיזוֹשֶׁהִי בְּעָיָה. מַסְפִּיק (enough) is a hif'il participle used as an adverb.

s.line: But day by day passed away,
and they still saw nothing before them but the scarlet fields.
s.note: מִלְּבַד = except / besides, a little more literary than חוּץ מִ. לֹא … דָּבָר = nothing; דָּבָר ("thing") turns negative with לֹא, like שׁוּם דָּבָר.

s.line: The Scarecrow began to grumble a bit.
s.note: לְרַטֵּן = to grumble, to complain under your breath, an everyday pi'el. The noun is רִטּוּן, and a habitual grumbler is רַטְנָן.

w: אֵין סָפֵק|no doubt|~idiom: lit. there is no doubt
s.line: “We have surely lost our way,” he said, “and unless we find it again in time to reach the Emerald City, I shall never get my brains.”
s.note: אִבֵּד (pi'el) = to lose something; אָבַד (pa'al) = to be lost, to perish. לְעוֹלָם לֹא = never (about the future), stronger than אַף פַּעַם לֹא. Without vowels, נמצא here is נִמְצָא "we will find" (pa'al), but it is also נִמְצָא "is found / is located" (nif'al).

s.line: “Nor I my heart,” declared the Tin Woodman.
s.note: הִכְרִיז = declared, announced. It is a news word: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל …; the noun הַכְרָזָה = announcement, and כָּרוֹז = a town crier.

w: נִדְמֶה לִי|it seems to me|nif'al · ד־מ־ה
s.line: “It seems to me I can scarcely wait till I get to Oz,
s.note: נִדְמֶה לִי = it seems to me, I think (nif'al, active meaning). בְּקֹשִׁי = hardly, barely, from קָשֶׁה: בְּקֹשִׁי שָׁמַעְתִּי = I could barely hear. מַצְלִיחַ לְ… = manage to (literally "succeed to").

s.line: and you must admit this is a very long journey.”
s.note: לְהוֹדוֹת has two meanings: לְהוֹדוֹת שֶׁ… = to admit that…, and לְהוֹדוֹת לְ… = to thank someone. תּוֹדָה comes from the same root.

w: אֵין לִי|I don't have|~lit. there is not to me
s.line: “You see,” said the Cowardly Lion, with a whimper, “I haven’t the courage to keep tramping forever, without getting anywhere at all.”
s.note: בְּלִי … לְשׁוּם מָקוֹם: שׁוּם also works after בְּלִי, not only after לֹא: "without (getting) to any place" = without getting anywhere. יְבָבָה = a whimper or wail; יִבֵּב = to whimper.

s.line: Then Dorothy lost heart.
s.note: הִתְיָאֵשׁ = to despair, to give up hope, a very common hitpa'el: אַל תִּתְיָאֵשׁ! (don't give up!). The noun is יֵאוּשׁ (despair), and מְיֹאָשׁ (pu'al participle) = desperate.

s.line: She sat down on the grass and looked at her companions,
and they sat down and looked at her,
and Toto found that for the first time in his life he was too tired to chase a butterfly that flew past his head.
s.note: עָיֵף מִדַּי כְּדֵי לִ… = too tired to…: מִדַּי (too much) + כְּדֵי + infinitive. רָדַף אַחֲרֵי = to chase, with אַחֲרֵי. בְּחַיָּיו (in his life) is one of the possessive endings that stay normal in modern Hebrew: פַּעַם רִאשׁוֹנָה בְּחַיַּי.

s.line: So he put out his tongue and panted and looked at Dorothy as if to ask what they should do next.
s.note: הוֹצִיא = took out, put out: the hif'il (causative) of יָצָא (went out), "made go out". הוֹצִיא לָשׁוֹן is also "stuck out his tongue" at someone. הִתְנַשֵּׁף = to pant, to gasp for breath (hitpa'el).

s.line: “Suppose we call the field mice,” she suggested.
s.note: אוּלַי + future = "how about we…", the normal way to make a suggestion: אוּלַי נֵלֵךְ לַיָּם? (shall we go to the beach?). קָרָא לְ… = to call someone (to come); קָרָא with אֶת means "to read".

s.line: “They could probably tell us the way to the Emerald City.”
s.note: אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לְ…? = "how does one get to…?", with a plural participle and no subject. This is exactly how you ask for directions in Israel: סְלִיחָה, אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לַתַּחֲנָה?. כַּנִּרְאֶה = probably, apparently.

s.line: “To be sure they could,” cried the Scarecrow.
s.note: בָּרוּר = clear, obvious; in speech it is simply "sure!" or "of course": – תָּבוֹא? – בָּרוּר!. In form it is a pa'ul (passive) participle, "made clear".

s.line: “Why didn’t we think of that before?”

w: מַלְכַּת הָעַכְבָּרִים|the Queen of the Mice
s.line: Dorothy blew the little whistle she had always carried about her neck since the Queen of the Mice had given it to her.
s.note: שָׁרַק בְּ… = to blow a whistle (literally "whistle with"); שָׁרַק alone = to whistle, and a מַשְׁרוֹקִית is what a referee blows. עָנַד is the verb for wearing jewelry, a watch, or something on a chain: עָנְדָה שַׁרְשֶׁרֶת. מֵאָז שֶׁ = since (in time).

s.line: In a few minutes they heard the pattering of tiny feet,
s.note: רַחַשׁ = a faint rustling or pattering sound. רַגְלַיִם is feminine (body parts that come in pairs usually are), hence קְטַנְטַנּוֹת.

s.line: and many of the small gray mice came running up to her.
s.note: בָּאוּ בְּרִיצָה = "came at a run". Hebrew often turns English "-ing" of manner into בְּ + noun: יָצְאָה בְּרִיצָה (ran out), נִכְנַס בִּצְעָקוֹת (came in shouting).

s.line: Among them was the Queen herself, who asked, in her squeaky little voice:
“What can I do for my friends?”
“We have lost our way,” said Dorothy.
“Can you tell us where the Emerald City is?”
s.note: נִמְצָא / נִמְצֵאת = "is (located)", the nif'al of מָצָא (found): literally "is found". It is the standard word for where something is: אֵיפֹה נִמְצֵאת הַתַּחֲנָה?. Here it is feminine to agree with עִיר.

s.line: “Certainly,” answered the Queen; “but it is a great way off, for you have had it at your backs all this time.”
s.note: The city is הִיא ("she") because עִיר is feminine, though it has no feminine ending; so are אֶרֶץ and דֶּרֶךְ. מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַגַּב = behind (your) back; מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַגַּב שֶׁלִּי also means "behind my back" in the sense of doing something secretly.

s.line: Then she noticed Dorothy’s Golden Cap, and said,
s.note: הִבְחִין בְּ… = to notice, with בְּ. The same verb with בֵּין means "to distinguish between": לְהַבְחִין בֵּין טוֹב לְרַע. The noun בְּחִינָה is an exam.

s.line: “Why don’t you use the charm of the Cap, and call the Winged Monkeys to you?
s.note: לָמָּה שֶׁלֹּא …? + future = "why don't you…?", a friendly suggestion: לָמָּה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא אִתָּנוּ?. הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ… = to use, always with בְּ. לַחַשׁ = a whispered magic spell, from לָחַשׁ (to whisper).

s.line: They will carry you to the City of Oz in less than an hour.”
“I didn’t know there was a charm,” answered Dorothy, in surprise.
s.note: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ: Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought, so "I didn't know there is". English shifts to "was". Same with הוּא אָמַר שֶׁהוּא עָיֵף = he said he was tired.

s.line: “What is it?”

w: מַלְכַּת הָעַכְבָּרִים|the Queen of the Mice
s.line: “It is written inside the Golden Cap,” replied the Queen of the Mice.
s.note: כָּתוּב = written, the pa'ul participle of כָּתַב. You see it everywhere: כָּתוּב שֶׁ… = "it says that…" (on a sign or in a text). הֵשִׁיב = replied, a slightly more literary twin of עָנָה; it is the hif'il of שָׁב (returned): "gave back (an answer)".

s.line: “But if you are going to call the Winged Monkeys we must run away,
s.note: עוֹמֵד / עוֹמֶדֶת לְ… + infinitive = "is about to": הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס עוֹמֵד לָצֵאת (the bus is about to leave). Very common in speech and in the news.

s.line: for they are full of mischief and think it great fun to plague us.”
s.note: לְהָצִיק לְ… = to bother, harass, pester someone (with לְ); הַטְרָדָה is the legal word, but הוּא מֵצִיק לִי is what kids say. כֵּיף = fun, borrowed from Arabic; כֵּיף לִי = I'm having a great time.

s.line: “Won’t they hurt me?” asked the girl anxiously.
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ… = to hurt or harm someone, with בְּ. It also means "to hit (a target)" and "to offend": נִפְגַּעְתִּי = I was hurt / offended. בִּדְאָגָה = with worry, בְּ + noun as an adverb.

w: מָה פִּתְאֹם|of course not|~idiom: lit. what suddenly
s.line: “Oh, no.
s.note: מָה פִּתְאֹם! = "no way! of course not!", literally "what (is this) suddenly". It is one of the most common Israeli reactions to a wrong idea.

s.line: They must obey the wearer of the Cap.
s.note: צִיֵּת לְ… = to obey (with לְ). חָבַשׁ is the verb for wearing a hat or helmet (חָבַשׁ קַסְדָּה); for clothes it is לָבַשׁ, for shoes נָעַל, for jewelry עָנַד. מִי שֶׁ = "whoever, the one who".

s.line: Good-bye!”
And she scampered out of sight, with all the mice hurrying after her.
s.note: לְהִתְרָאוֹת = goodbye, literally "to see each other (again)": a hitpa'el of רָאָה, where the hitpa'el means "each other". נֶעֱלַם = disappeared, nif'al with an active meaning.

s.line: Dorothy looked inside the Golden Cap and saw some words written upon the lining.
s.note: Without vowels, בטנה is בִּטְנָה (the lining of a garment) or בִּטְנָהּ (her belly). Both come from בֶּטֶן (belly, inside). הֵצִיץ = to peek, to take a quick look.

s.line: These, she thought, must be the charm,
so she read the directions carefully and put the Cap upon her head.
s.note: הוֹרָאוֹת = instructions, directions (הוֹרָאוֹת הַפְעָלָה = operating instructions). The singular הוֹרָאָה also means "teaching", and מוֹרֶה (teacher) is from the same root.

s.line: “Ep-pe, pep-pe, kak-ke!” she said, standing on her left foot.
s.note: כְּשֶׁהִיא עוֹמֶדֶת = "standing", literally "while she stands". English "-ing" describing what someone is doing at the same time becomes כְּשֶׁ + present. רֶגֶל שְׂמֹאל / רֶגֶל יָמִין: שְׂמֹאל and יָמִין work as nouns placed after the body part.

s.line: “What did you say?” asked the Scarecrow, who did not know what she was doing.
“Hil-lo, hol-lo, hel-lo!” Dorothy went on, standing this time on her right foot.
“Hello!” replied the Tin Woodman calmly.
s.note: Israelis answer the phone with הַלּוֹ, but greet each other with שָׁלוֹם or הַי; הֶלוֹ here keeps Baum's joke. שַׁלְוָה = calm, tranquility, related to שָׁלֵו (calm, serene).

s.line: “Ziz-zy, zuz-zy, zik!” said Dorothy, who was now standing on both feet.
This ended the saying of the charm,
s.note: הִסְתַּיֵּם = to end, come to an end (hitpa'el; the ת swaps places with the ס). Compare סִיֵּם (pi'el) = to finish something. בְּכָךְ = "with that, thereby", a written-style word.

w: וּמַשַּׁק כְּנָפַיִם|and flapping of wings|~set phrase
s.line: and they heard a great chattering and flapping of wings, as the band of Winged Monkeys flew up to them.
s.note: מַשַּׁק כְּנָפַיִם = the beating of wings, a fixed phrase; the "butterfly effect" is אֶפֶקְט הַפַּרְפַּר, and people also speak of מַשַּׁק כַּנְפֵי הַפַּרְפַּר. לַהֲקָה = a flock (of birds) and also a music band.

s.line: The King bowed low before Dorothy, and asked,
“What is your command?”
s.note: צִוָּה = to command, order (pi'el). The noun is צַו (an order, also a legal order: צַו מַעְצָר = arrest warrant) and מִצְוָה (a commandment, a good deed). In a restaurant you may still hear the old-fashioned מָה תְּצַוֶּה? = what would you like?

s.line: “We wish to go to the Emerald City,” said the child, “and we have lost our way.”
“We will carry you,” replied the King,
s.note: נִשָּׂא is a nice case of two forms that look exactly the same, even with vowels: "we will carry" (pa'al future of נָשָׂא) and "he was carried / he married" (nif'al past). Only the subject tells you which: here אֲנַחְנוּ is understood.

s.line: and no sooner had he spoken than two of the Monkeys caught Dorothy in their arms and flew away with her.
s.note: בְּרֶגַע שֶׁ… = "the moment that, as soon as": תִּתְקַשֵּׁר בְּרֶגַע שֶׁאַתָּה מַגִּיעַ (call as soon as you arrive). It is the everyday equivalent of English "no sooner … than".

s.line: Others took the Scarecrow and the Woodman and the Lion,

w: בְּכָל כּוֹחוֹ|with all his might|~idiom: lit. with all his strength
s.line: and one little Monkey seized Toto and flew after them, although the dog tried hard to bite him.
s.note: לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ… = although; before a noun, לַמְרוֹת = despite: לַמְרוֹת הַגֶּשֶׁם. חָטַף = snatched, grabbed; in the news it means "kidnapped" (חֲטִיפָה = kidnapping), and חָטַף in slang also means "got hit, caught it".

s.line: The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman were rather frightened at first,
s.note: נִבְהַל = got scared, took fright: a nif'al with an active meaning, so no underline. Its partner הִבְהִיל (hif'il) = to frighten someone, and בֶּהָלָה = panic. דִּי = rather, quite: דִּי טוֹב = pretty good.

s.line: for they remembered how badly the Winged Monkeys had treated them before;
s.note: הִתְנַהֵג אֶל = to treat (someone), literally "behave toward". הִתְנַהֵג alone = to behave: תִּתְנַהֵג יָפֶה! (behave yourself!). The noun is הִתְנַהֲגוּת (behavior).

s.line: but they saw that no harm was intended,
s.note: English "no harm was intended" is a passive; Hebrew turns it into an active sentence with a subject: "no one intends to hurt them". הִתְכַּוֵּן = to mean, to intend: לֹא הִתְכַּוַּנְתִּי = I didn't mean it.

w: בְּמַצַּב רוּחַ|in a mood|~idiom: lit. in a state of spirit
s.line: so they rode through the air quite cheerfully,
s.note: מַצַּב רוּחַ = mood: יֵשׁ לִי מַצַּב רוּחַ טוֹב (I'm in a good mood). טָס = to fly, especially by plane: אֲנִי טָס לְאֵילַת. A bird or a monkey can also עָף.

s.line: and had a fine time looking at the pretty gardens and woods far below them.
s.note: נֶהֱנָה = to enjoy, a nif'al with an active meaning; what you enjoy takes מִ: נֶהֱנֵיתִי מֵהַסֶּרֶט, or an infinitive as here. הִסְתַּכֵּל עַל = to look at, with עַל, while הִבִּיט takes בְּ.

s.line: Dorothy found herself riding easily between two of the biggest Monkeys,
s.note: הַגְּדוֹלִים בְּיוֹתֵר = the biggest: the written superlative is adjective + בְּיוֹתֵר; in speech people say הֲכִי גְּדוֹלִים. בְּנוֹחוּת = comfortably, from נוֹחַ (comfortable).

s.line: one of them the King himself.
They had made a chair of their hands and were careful not to hurt her.
s.note: נִזְהַר = to be careful (nif'al, active): תִּזָּהֵר! = watch out! הִכְאִיב לְ… = to cause pain to, with לְ; כּוֹאֵב לִי = it hurts me. Compare פָּגַע בְּ (to harm) earlier in the chapter.

s.line: “Why do you have to obey the charm of the Golden Cap?” she asked.
“That is a long story,” answered the King, with a winged laugh;
s.note: מְכֻנָּף (winged) is a pu'al participle, "provided with wings", like הַקּוֹפִים הַמְּכֻנָּפִים in the title. "A winged laugh" is Baum's playful phrase; it sounds just as odd in Hebrew.

w: אַעֲבִיר אֶת הַזְּמַן|I will pass the time|~idiom
s.line: “but as we have a long journey before us, I will pass the time by telling you about it, if you wish.”
s.note: לְהַעֲבִיר אֶת הַזְּמַן = to pass the time; הֶעֱבִיר is the hif'il of עָבַר (passed), "made pass". בְּכָךְ שֶׁ… = "by (doing)…": הוּא עָזַר לִי בְּכָךְ שֶׁהִסְבִּיר. מִכֵּיוָן שֶׁ = since, because, a little more formal than כִּי.

s.line: “I shall be glad to hear it,” she replied.
s.note: אֶשְׂמַח + infinitive = "I'd be happy to", the polite way to accept or offer: אֶשְׂמַח לַעֲזֹר. In a business email אֶשְׂמַח אִם … = "I'd appreciate it if…".

s.line: “Once,” began the leader, “we were a free people, living happily in the great forest,
s.note: פָּתַח = opened, and also "began (a speech or story)": הוּא פָּתַח וְאָמַר. מַנְהִיג = leader (hif'il participle of נ־ה־ג, "one who leads"); נָהַג (pa'al) = to drive, and הִתְנַהֵג = to behave.

s.line: flying from tree to tree, eating nuts and fruit,

w: מָה שֶׁבָּא לָנוּ|whatever we felt like|~idiom: lit. what came to us
s.line: and doing just as we pleased without calling anybody master.
s.note: בָּא לִי = "I feel like (it)", literally "it comes to me": בָּא לְךָ פִּיצָה? (do you feel like pizza?), לֹא בָּא לִי (I don't feel like it). It is colloquial but everywhere in Israeli speech.

s.line: Perhaps some of us were rather too full of mischief at times,
s.note: שׁוֹבָב = naughty, mischievous, said of children with affection: אֵיזֶה שׁוֹבָב!. The abstract noun is שׁוֹבָבוּת (mischief), which the Queen of the Mice used above.

w: הָיוּ לָהֶן|they had|~lit. there were to them (fem.)
s.line: flying down to pull the tails of the animals that had no wings, chasing birds, and throwing nuts at the people who walked in the forest.
s.note: מָשַׁךְ בְּ… = to pull at something, with בְּ: מָשַׁךְ בַּשַּׂעֲרוֹת שֶׁלָּהּ. הָיוּ לָהֶן: לָהֶן is feminine because חַיּוֹת (animals) is feminine. עָט = to swoop down, as a bird of prey does; it is also used figuratively: עָט עַל הָאֹכֶל = pounced on the food.

s.line: But we were careless and happy and full of fun, and enjoyed every minute of the day.
s.note: חַסְרֵי דְּאָגוֹת and מְלֵאֵי שִׂמְחָה: adjectives like חָסֵר (lacking) and מָלֵא (full) go into construct form before a noun: חֲסַר סַבְלָנוּת (impatient), מָלֵא חַיִּים (full of life).

s.line: This was many years ago, long before Oz came out of the clouds to rule over this land.
s.note: לִפְנֵי + a time = "ago": לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה (a year ago); לִפְנֵי שֶׁ + a verb = "before": לִפְנֵי שֶׁאוֹז יָרַד. מָלַךְ עַל = to reign over; מֶלֶךְ and מַלְכָּה share the root.

s.line: “There lived here then, away at the North, a beautiful princess, who was also a powerful sorceress.
s.note: רַב עָצְמָה / רַבַּת עָצְמָה = powerful, mighty, a written-register phrase (construct of רַב + עָצְמָה, power). News uses it for storms and armies: סְעָרָה רַבַּת עָצְמָה. Note the word order: the verb גָּרָה comes before its subject, as in English "there lived".

s.line: All her magic was used to help the people,
and she was never known to hurt anyone who was good.
s.note: English "she was never known to…" is passive; Hebrew uses a plural verb with no subject, "they never heard that she…". This subjectless <t>שָׁמְעוּ</t> / <t>אוֹמְרִים</t> is the usual Hebrew way to avoid a passive.

s.line: Her name was Gayelette,
and she lived in a handsome palace built from great blocks of ruby.
s.note: נִבְנָה = was built, the nif'al (passive) of בָּנָה. מְפֹאָר = magnificent, splendid, a pu'al participle in form. אֹדֶם = ruby; the same word, from אָדֹם (red), is also everyday Hebrew for lipstick.

s.line: Everyone loved her,
but her greatest sorrow was that she could find no one to love in return,
since all the men were much too stupid and ugly to mate with one so beautiful and wise.
s.note: מְכֹעָר (ugly) is a pu'al participle in form, like מְפֹאָר above: the pu'al often gives adjectives of state. הִתְחַתֵּן עִם = to marry someone, with עִם; חֲתֻנָּה = wedding. מִישֶׁהִי is the feminine of מִישֶׁהוּ.

s.line: At last, however, she found a boy who was handsome and manly and wise beyond his years.
s.note: מֵעֵבֶר לְ… = beyond: מֵעֵבֶר לַיָּם (overseas). For a child who acts older than his age, Israelis also say בּוֹגֵר לְגִילוֹ (mature for his age). גַּבְרִי = manly, from גֶּבֶר; נָשִׁי = feminine.

s.line: Gayelette made up her mind that when he grew to be a man she would make him her husband,
s.note: כְּשֶׁהוּא יִגְדַּל: after כְּשֶׁ about the future, Hebrew uses the future tense ("when he will grow"), and the whole plan stays in the future even though the story is in the past. הָיָה לְ… = to become: יִהְיֶה לְגֶבֶר = will become a man.

s.line: so she took him to her ruby palace and used all her magic powers to make him as strong and good and lovely as any woman could wish.
s.note: מַקְסִים = charming, lovely: the hif'il participle of the root of קֶסֶם (magic), "one who casts a spell", a nice fit in this sentence. הָיְתָה רוֹצָה: הָיָה + a participle gives "would": הָיִיתִי בָּא = I would come.

s.line: When he grew to manhood, Quelala, as he was called, was said to be the best and wisest man in all the land,
s.note: Two more subjectless plurals for English passives: אָמְרוּ שֶׁ = "he was said to…" and כָּךְ קָרְאוּ לוֹ = "as he was called". הִתְבַּגֵּר = to grow up, from בּוֹגֵר (adult); a teenager is מִתְבַּגֵּר.

s.line: while his manly beauty was so great that Gayelette loved him dearly, and hastened to make everything ready for the wedding.
“My grandfather was at that time the King of the Winged Monkeys which lived in the forest near Gayelette’s palace,
and the old fellow loved a joke better than a good dinner.
s.note: יוֹתֵר מִ… = more than; the מִ attaches straight to the noun: יוֹתֵר מֵאֲרוּחָה. הַזָּקֵן = the old man; in slang הַזָּקֵן שֶׁלִּי = "my old man", my dad.

s.line: One day, just before the wedding, my grandfather was flying out with his band when he saw Quelala walking beside the river.
s.note: מַמָּשׁ = really, right, exactly: מַמָּשׁ לִפְנֵי (just before), מַמָּשׁ יָפֶה (really nice). טִיֵּל = to stroll, take a walk, also to travel or hike: טִיַּלְנוּ בַּגָּלִיל.

s.line: He was dressed in a rich costume of pink silk and purple velvet,
s.note: לָבוּשׁ = dressed, wearing: the pa'ul participle of לָבַשׁ, describing a state. מְהֻדָּר = elegant, fancy (a pu'al participle): מִסְעָדָה מְהֻדֶּרֶת. The pu'al's ֻ vowel under the first letter is a good clue to a passive form.

s.line: and my grandfather thought he would see what he could do.
At his word the band flew down and seized Quelala,
carried him in their arms until they were over the middle of the river, and then dropped him into the water.
s.note: הִפִּיל = dropped, made fall: the hif'il (causative) of נָפַל (fell). The נ of the root disappears into the dagesh of the פּ. Same pattern: נָסַע → הִסִּיעַ (gave someone a ride).

s.line: “‘Swim out, my fine fellow,’ cried my grandfather, ‘and see if the water has spotted your clothes.’
s.note: שְׂחֵה is the imperative of שָׂחָה (to swim); infinitive לִשְׂחוֹת, and swimming is שְׂחִיָּה. הִכְתִּים = to stain, from כֶּתֶם (a stain, spot). Note that מַיִם is plural in Hebrew, so the verb is plural: הַמַּיִם הִכְתִּימוּ.

s.line: Quelala was much too wise not to swim,
s.note: … מִדַּי מִכְּדֵי לְ… = "too … to …", the written form of מִדַּי כְּדֵי: הוּא עָיֵף מִדַּי מִכְּדֵי לִנְהֹג (he is too tired to drive).

s.line: and he was not in the least spoiled by all his good fortune.
s.note: מְפֻנָּק = spoiled (a child, a pampered person): pu'al participle of פִּנֵּק (to pamper), an everyday pair: פִּנַּקְתִּי אֶת עַצְמִי (I treated myself). הָפַךְ … לְ… = turned (something) into.

w: פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם|the surface of the water|~lit. the face of the water
s.line: He laughed, when he came to the top of the water, and swam in to shore.
s.note: פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם = the surface of the water, literally "the face of the water". פְּנֵי is used for many surfaces: פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה (the face of the earth), פְּנֵי הַשֶּׁטַח (ground level).

s.line: But when Gayelette came running out to him she found his silks and velvet all ruined by the river.
s.note: נֶהֱרַס = was destroyed, ruined: the nif'al (passive) of הָרַס (destroyed). You will hear הָרַסְתָּ לִי אֶת הַיּוֹם = you ruined my day.

s.line: “The princess was angry, and she knew, of course, who did it.
s.note: כָּעַס = to be angry, a pa'al verb (where English uses "be" + adjective); with the person you are angry at: כָּעַס עַל. The adjective is כּוֹעֵס, and the noun כַּעַס.

s.line: She had all the Winged Monkeys brought before her,
and she said at first that their wings should be tied and they should be treated as they had treated Quelala, and dropped in the river.
s.note: צָרִיךְ + infinitive with no subject = "one must, it should be done": צָרִיךְ לִקְשֹׁר = "(they) should be tied". This is how Hebrew handles a whole chain of English passives in one go.

s.line: But my grandfather pleaded hard,
s.note: הִתְחַנֵּן = to beg, plead (hitpa'el); "plead with someone" = הִתְחַנֵּן לִפְנֵי.

s.line: for he knew the Monkeys would drown in the river with their wings tied,
s.note: קְשׁוּרוֹת = tied, a pa'ul participle, feminine plural because כָּנָף (wing) is feminine. טָבַע = to drown or sink; טָבַע also means "sank" for ships. Without vowels, טבע can also be טֶבַע (nature).

w: מִלָּה טוֹבָה|a good word|~idiom: put in a good word
s.line: and Quelala said a kind word for them also;
s.note: לְהַגִּיד / לוֹמַר מִלָּה טוֹבָה עַל = to put in a good word for someone, used just as in English: תַּגִּיד עָלַי מִלָּה טוֹבָה לַמְּנַהֵל.

w: שֶׁבְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר|that in the end|~idiom: lit. at the end of the matter
s.line: so that Gayelette finally spared them,
s.note: בְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר = in the end, ultimately, a set phrase that sounds slightly bookish but is common in speeches and articles. חָס עַל = to spare, to have pity on; a related expression is חַס וְחָלִילָה (God forbid).

w: מֵאָז וָהָלְאָה|ever after|~idiom: lit. from then onward
s.line: on condition that the Winged Monkeys should ever after do three times the bidding of the owner of the Golden Cap.
s.note: בִּתְנַאי שֶׁ… = on condition that, provided that. מִלֵּא פְּקֻדָּה = to carry out an order; מִלֵּא (pi'el of מָלֵא, full) also means "to fill" and "to fill out": לְמַלֵּא טֹפֶס (fill out a form).

s.line: This Cap had been made for a wedding present to Quelala,
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה = was made, the nif'al of עָשָׂה. It also means "became": נַעֲשָׂה קַר (it got cold), so context decides between "was made" and "became".

s.line: and it is said to have cost the princess half her kingdom.
s.note: עָלָה = "went up", but also "cost": כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה? (how much does it cost?), זֶה עָלָה לִי מִילְיוֹן. אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ = "they say that, it is said that", again a subjectless plural.

s.line: Of course my grandfather and all the other Monkeys at once agreed to the condition,
s.note: הִסְכִּים לְ… = to agree to something; "agree with someone" is הִסְכִּים עִם. The noun הֶסְכֵּם = an agreement, a treaty, often in the news.

w: יִהְיֶה מִי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה|whoever he may be|~idiom: lit. be who he may be
s.line: and that is how it happens that we are three times the slaves of the owner of the Golden Cap, whosoever he may be.”
s.note: יִהְיֶה מִי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה = whoever it may be; also יִהְיֶה מָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה = whatever happens, come what may.

s.line: “And what became of them?” asked Dorothy, who had been greatly interested in the story.
s.note: הִקְשִׁיב לְ… = to listen to (with לְ); שָׁמַע is "to hear". בְּעִנְיָן = with interest; עִנְיָן also means "matter, affair": זֶה לֹא הָעִנְיָן = that's not the point.

s.line: “Quelala being the first owner of the Golden Cap,” replied the Monkey, “he was the first to lay his wishes upon us.
s.note: בְּעָלִים = owner: it looks plural but is used for one owner too, and the adjective is singular: הַבְּעָלִים הָרִאשׁוֹן, בַּעַל הַבַּיִת or בַּעֲלֵי הַבַּיִת (the landlord). דָּרַשׁ מִ… = to demand of someone; מֵאִתָּנוּ is the formal form of מִמֶּנּוּ (from us).

s.line: As his bride could not bear the sight of us,
s.note: לֹא יָכוֹל לִסְבֹּל = can't stand: אֲנִי לֹא סוֹבֵל אֶת הַחֹם (I can't stand the heat). סָבַל also means "to suffer" (סֵבֶל = suffering). כַּלָּה = bride, and also daughter-in-law.

s.line: he called us all to him in the forest after he had married her
and ordered us always to keep where she could never again set eyes on a Winged Monkey,
s.note: צִוָּה עַל = to order someone, with עַל: הַמְּפַקֵּד צִוָּה עֲלֵיהֶם לַעֲצֹר. מָקוֹם שֶׁבּוֹ = "a place in which" = where; in speech people often just say אֵיפֹה שֶׁ.

s.line: which we were glad to do, for we were all afraid of her.
s.note: בְּשִׂמְחָה = gladly, with pleasure, also the polite way to say yes to a request: – תּוּכַל לַעֲזֹר? – בְּשִׂמְחָה!. פָּחַד מִ… = to be afraid of, with מִ.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “This was all we ever had to do until the Golden Cap fell into the hands of the Wicked Witch of the West,
s.note: נִדְרַשׁ = was required, the nif'al (passive) of דָּרַשׁ (demanded): נִדְרַשְׁנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת = we were required to do. Job ads say דָּרוּשׁ / דְּרוּשָׁה = "wanted", the pa'ul participle of the same verb.

s.line: who made us enslave the Winkies,
s.note: הִכְרִיחַ = to force, compel someone to do something; the adjective מֻכְרָח (hof'al participle) = forced, "have to": אֲנִי מֻכְרָח לָלֶכֶת (I must go).

s.line: and afterward drive Oz himself out of the Land of the West.
s.note: גֵּרֵשׁ = to expel, drive out, deport (pi'el); a person who was deported גֹּרַשׁ (pu'al, the passive partner). גֵּרוּשִׁין = divorce, from the same root.

s.line: Now the Golden Cap is yours,
s.note: שַׁיָּךְ לְ… = belongs to: זֶה שַׁיָּךְ לִי (that's mine). In speech לֹא שַׁיָּךְ also means "irrelevant, out of the question".

s.line: and three times you have the right to lay your wishes upon us.”
s.note: זְכוּת = a right; זְכֻיּוֹת אָדָם = human rights. מִשְׁאָלָה = a wish, from שָׁאַל (asked); a birthday wish is מִשְׁאָלָה, while אִחוּל is a wish you give to someone else.

s.line: As the Monkey King finished his story Dorothy looked down and saw the green, shining walls of the Emerald City before them.
s.note: חוֹמָה is a city wall or rampart (חוֹמוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַיִם), while קִיר is the wall of a room. מַבְרִיק = shiny, and in speech also "brilliant": רַעְיוֹן מַבְרִיק (a brilliant idea).

s.line: She wondered at the rapid flight of the Monkeys,
s.note: הִתְפַּלֵּא עַל = to be amazed at, to wonder at; from the same root as פֶּלֶא (a wonder) and נִפְלָא (wonderful). שֶׁבָּהּ = "with which": the בָּהּ refers back to מְהִירוּת (feminine).

s.line: but was glad the journey was over.
s.note: נִגְמַר = ended, ran out: nif'al with an active meaning, no underline. נִגְמַר לִי הַחָלָב = I ran out of milk. Its pa'al partner גָּמַר = to finish (something).

s.line: The strange creatures set the travelers down carefully before the gate of the City,
s.note: הוֹרִיד = to take down, put down, the hif'il of יָרַד (went down). Everyday uses: תּוֹרִיד אוֹתִי כָּאן (drop me off here), לְהוֹרִיד אַפְּלִיקַצְיָה (download an app).

s.line: the King bowed low to Dorothy,
and then flew swiftly away, followed by all his band.
“That was a good ride,” said the little girl.
s.note: זֹאת הָיְתָה: the pointer זֹאת and the verb agree with טִיסָה (feminine). With a masculine noun it would be זֶה הָיָה טִיּוּל טוֹב. טִיסָה is the noun of טָס (to fly).

s.line: “Yes, and a quick way out of our troubles,” replied the Lion.
s.note: צָרָה = trouble, distress: יֵשׁ לִי צָרוֹת (I've got problems), לָצֵאת מִצָּרָה = to get out of trouble. The adjective צַר = narrow, and צַר לִי = I'm sorry.

w: אֵיזֶה מַזָּל|how lucky|~idiom: lit. what luck
s.line: “How lucky it was you brought away that wonderful Cap!”
s.note: אֵיזֶה מַזָּל! = how lucky! אֵיזֶה + noun is the everyday exclamation: אֵיזֶה יוֹפִי! (great!), אֵיזוֹ בּוּשָׁה! (what a shame!). לָקַחְתְּ ends in a pointed תְּ because Dorothy is "you" feminine.
